sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Salient Initial Findings
sections.description: Outlines the patient’s symptoms, examination, and first-line investigations that framed the problem as a multisystem disorder with ineffective erythropoiesis, hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis, neuropathy, and metabolic bone disease.
subtopics: History: 5-year progressive fatigue/weakness, recent functional decline, exertional dyspnoea, chest discomfort, weight loss, anorexia
Examination: pallor, icterus, premature greying, knuckle hyperpigmentation, atrophic glossitis, thoracic scoliosis, thenar atrophy, hepatomegaly, reduced basal breath sounds
Hematology: pancytopenia with low reticulocyte count (0.39%); peripheral smear showing dimorphic RBCs, basophilic stippling, Cabot rings, hypersegmented neutrophils
Nutritional profile: severe vitamin B12 and folate deficiency; iron studies with high serum iron and ferritin consistent with ineffective erythropoiesis
Bone marrow: trilineage hematopoiesis with erythroid hyperplasia, increased iron stores; no malignancy/dysplasia; normal cytogenetics

Hemolysis assessment: elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin; positive DAT (IgG 2+) but incongruent with low reticulocyte response and marrow findings (favoring ineffective erythropoiesis over immune destruction)
Hepatic involvement: ultrasound hepatosplenomegaly; transient elastography showing grade II steatosis and cirrhosis (18.1 kPa); negative autoimmune and viral hepatitis workup
Pulmonary involvement: PET-CT with diffuse ground-glass and fibrotic/subpleural atelectatic changes; no malignancy or granulomatous disease
Neuromuscular and bone health: asymmetric sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy on EMG/NCS; vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypocalcaemia, osteoporosis on DEXA
Early synthesis: multisystem features out of proportion to nutritional deficiency alone, prompting consideration of an inherited or syndromic etiology

sections.description: Details how common and life-threatening causes were prioritized and excluded, and how the pattern of early-onset fibrosis with cytopenia prompted suspicion for a telomere biology disorder (TBD).
subtopics: Hematologic differentials: megaloblastic anemia (from B12/folate deficiency) versus aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, marrow infiltration, and hemolytic anemia

Evidence integration: marrow erythroid hyperplasia and low retic consistent with ineffective erythropoiesis; normal cytogenetics argues against MDS; DAT positivity insufficient to diagnose autoimmune hemolysis given marrow and retic data

Malabsorption and autoimmune gastritis: normal EGD; duodenal biopsy with reduced parietal cells consistent with impaired intrinsic factor production; explains deficiency but not full multisystem picture
Systemic inflammation/autoimmunity: elevated inflammatory markers yet negative ANA/AIH panel and lack of systemic features reduce likelihood of autoimmune cytopenia or connective tissue disease
Infections and infiltrative disease: broad infectious workup largely negative (EBV IgG only); PET-CT without malignancy or granulomas
Unexplained hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis in a young adult: cryptogenic cirrhosis and interstitial lung disease raise suspicion for inherited disorders

Trigger to genetic testing: early-onset multisystem involvement (cytopenia, hepatic/pulmonary fibrosis, premature greying, osteoporosis) with no unifying acquired cause; consider TBD despite absence of classical DC mucocutaneous triad
Test selection: clinical exome sequencing to survey telomere-related genes given phenotypic breadth and variable penetrance

sections.section_title: Telomere Biology and PARN: Focused Pathophysiology for This Case
sections.description: Provides the mechanistic background necessary to understand how PARN dysfunction leads to short telomeres and organ-specific failure, mapping directly to the patient’s phenotype.
subtopics: Telomere maintenance: telomeres shorten with replication; telomerase (TERT/TERC) counters attrition in highly proliferative tissues (marrow, epithelium, hepatocytes)
PARN function: a 3′-5′ exoribonuclease required for deadenylation and 3′-end maturation/stability of TERC; PARN deficiency reduces functional telomerase RNA and impairs telomere maintenance

Genotype–phenotype correlations: biallelic PARN variants cause recessive DC/HH; monoallelic variants often cause pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure (PFBMFT4); hepatic fibrosis is increasingly recognized in TBDs

Organ-level consequences relevant to this patient: marrow—reduced stem cell replicative reserve (vulnerability to cytopenias and BM failure); lung—type II pneumocyte senescence and fibrotic remodeling; liver—progenitor exhaustion and fibrosis/cirrhosis; skin/hair—premature greying and subtle mucocutaneous changes
Stressors unmasking TBD: severe B12 deficiency can precipitate or magnify cytopenias in a marrow already constrained by short telomeres, explaining disproportionate illness severity

Variable penetrance and expressivity: effects of gene dose (monoallelic vs biallelic), environmental modifiers, and possible somatic genetic rescue leading to heterogeneous adult presentations without the classical DC triad

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Synthesis: Assigning a Working TBD Diagnosis with a Monoallelic PARN Variant (VUS)
sections.description: Explains how the clinicians integrated genotype and phenotype to reach a working diagnosis of a telomere biology disorder and outlines confirmatory/adjunct tests that refine classification and guide family counseling.
subtopics: Genetic finding: monoallelic PARN missense variant c.613T>C (p.Cys205Arg) in the R3H domain (nucleic acid-binding region), affecting a highly conserved residue

ACMG/AMP evidence applied: PM1 (critical functional domain), PM2 (absent/rare in population databases), PP2 (low benign missense rate and missense mechanism), PP3 (damaging in silico predictions) → Variant of Uncertain Significance overall

Phenotype–genotype concordance: young adult with cytopenia, hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis, and premature greying—within the PARN/TBD spectrum—supporting a working clinical diagnosis despite VUS status

Confirmatory/adjunct investigations recommended: leukocyte telomere length by flow-FISH in multiple subsets; segregation analysis in relatives; functional assays (PARN activity or TERC maturation where available); periodic re-analysis of variant as databases evolve

Distinguishing primary deficiency from predisposition: B12 deficiency likely explains acute ineffective erythropoiesis, while the PARN variant provides a unifying predisposition to organ fibrosis and marrow vulnerability
Diagnostic pitfalls: overcalling autoimmune hemolysis based solely on DAT positivity; dismissing TBD in the absence of the DC triad; attributing multisystem disease solely to nutritional deficiency

sections.section_title: Management Strategy and Long-term Surveillance in TBD
sections.description: Details immediate care delivered in this case, organ-specific management principles for PARN-associated TBDs, and longitudinal strategies including transplant considerations and genetic counseling.
subtopics: Acute/supportive care provided: parenteral B12 repletion (loading then maintenance), folate supplementation, transfusions for symptomatic anemia, vitamin D/calcium, electrolyte correction, physiotherapy
Hematology: close monitoring for evolving marrow failure; avoid myelotoxic drugs; individualized use of growth factors; early referral to transplant centers if progressive cytopenias emerge

HSCT considerations: indication is progressive BMF; pretransplant telomere length testing; reduced-intensity conditioning to limit toxicity; careful donor selection (avoid relatives with short telomeres/variants); anticipate pulmonary/hepatic complications

Pulmonary fibrosis care: multidisciplinary ILD management; consider antifibrotics (pirfenidone or nintedanib) when criteria met; vaccinate, pulmonary rehab, oxygen as needed; early transplant discussions

Hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis care: hepatology comanagement; lifestyle and metabolic risk modification (for steatosis); variceal screening, HCC surveillance, management of portal hypertension; transplant candidacy in advanced disease

Bone and neuromuscular health: treat osteoporosis (vitamin D/calcium; consider antiresorptives as indicated), fall prevention, analgesia and neurorehabilitation; reassess neuropathy after B12 repletion
Prevention and lifestyle: smoking cessation; minimize alcohol; vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis A/B); infection prophylaxis as indicated

Genetic counseling: autosomal dominant risk with variable penetrance for monoallelic PARN; cascade testing and telomere length assessment in relatives; reproductive counseling including options such as PGT

sections.description: Summarizes the clinical course and distills actionable lessons on when to suspect TBDs, how to avoid pitfalls, and prognostic factors relevant to PARN-associated disease.
subtopics: Case outcome: symptomatic improvement and stable counts after deficiency correction; ongoing surveillance of hepatic, pulmonary, and hematologic status
Prognosis in PARN-associated TBDs: variable; influenced by telomere length, organ involvement at diagnosis, and progression of pulmonary/hepatic fibrosis or marrow failure

When to suspect a TBD: early-onset unexplained cytopenias plus cryptogenic liver disease and/or interstitial lung disease; premature greying or subtle mucocutaneous signs; strong response to nutrition yet disproportionate multisystem disease

Common pitfalls: attributing all findings to vitamin deficiency; relying on DAT positivity to diagnose autoimmune hemolysis; deferring genetic evaluation due to absent family history or classic DC triad

Operational pearls: order telomere length testing early in young adults with organ fibrosis plus cytopenia; coordinate multidisciplinary care; screen related stem cell donors for short telomeres/variants before selection; re-review VUS periodically as evidence accrues
